newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: World Bank reviews Ivorian cocoa, coffee auctions.
newsitem.headline: World Bank reviews Ivorian cocoa, coffee auctions.

text.p: The World Bank and other donors are studying ways of modifying Ivory Coast's cocoa and coffee contract auctions after Caistab marketing agency complaints that a few shippers had dominated business by posting excessive bids.
"Caistab says it tends to induce the bidders to over-bid," said Shigeo Katsu, head of the World Bank mission in Abidjan.
"Different options are being discussed but there are no firm proposals," he told Reuters.

A European Union official said one option was for the Caistab to take bids from at least five firms in each auction session and then share the export contracts between them on a pro-rata basis, with the highest bidder getting the most.
The current system allocates contracts in two daily sessions to the highest bidder prepared to take the full amount on offer.
Exporters said two European-backed firms had been bidding unrealistically high prices to secure export contracts, and other firms had been unable to compete.

"There is a double speculation here because the futures market is a type of speculation and the same goes for the auctioning system," Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze told a Common Fund for Commodities meeting in Abidjan last month.

The Caistab launched the auction last May, six months later than planned, as part of a $150 million World Bank loan deal with Ivory Coast. The World Bank, European Union and other donor agencies reviewed its performance last month.
Katsu said the Bank was receptive to Caistab comments about the auction but added that the evaluation was made at an early stage and further studies would be needed.

The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have been pushing for liberalisation of Ivory Coast's cocoa and coffee sector in a bid to improve marketing transparency and efficiency and to cut costs so the farmer can get more of the world price.
Some exporters said the Caistab's previous telephone-based method of allocating export contracts was unfair because there was no guarantee deals were done on price alone.
They say the auction is a good idea in principle but that it needs to be modified to keep prices realistic.

Another donor-backed reform involves the forward sale of at least 70 percent of the forecast cocoa crop before the season starts. Sources close to the July review said the Caistab's advance sales programme appeared to be on track.
They said the Caistab had sold 600,000 tonnes of 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) crop using its traditional "over-the-phone" method before the auction was in place.
Only around 50,000 tonnes more had been sold through the auction between May and July, they added.
The coming main crop is forecast at 800,000-900,000 tonnes. The mid-crop is normally in a 100,000-200,000 tonne range.
Caistab chief executive Rene Amany was not immediately available for comment.
